evals.prompt: I'm writing a blog post about why our Kafka consumers fall behind. Setup: the checkout service publishes order events to a topic with 6 partitions at about 1,200 msgs/s. Two consumer groups read it: fulfillment (3 consumers, each does ~450/s) and analytics (1 consumer, ~1,500/s). I want one interactive figure that shows what happens to fulfillment's lag when one of its consumers dies. Single HTML file, dark, the polished isometric look.
evals.expected_output: A single standalone dark HTML page built with scripts/build.mjs from a .spec.mjs (no hand-written page). The spec has a producer, a kafka node with partitions: 6, and consumers in two groups (fulfillment ×3, analytics ×1) with rates sized from the stated numbers, using sim.per so on-screen packets stay under ~30/s while the readout shows the real ~1,200/s. A scenario with named phases (steady → consumer lost → recovery) fails one fulfillment consumer and later recovers it, with `say` lines that tell the reader what to watch (bright record cells, the fulfillment cursor falling behind while analytics' stays at the head). The response sizes the rates against partition assignment (6 partitions over 3 consumers is 2 each; over 2 survivors it is 3 each, so 3 × 200/s = 600/s against ~450/s capacity, and lag must grow during the incident and drain after recovery). `node scripts/build.mjs <spec> --check` was run, and its phase numbers (lag per phase, in/s) match what the caption and narration claim. Its only warnings, if any, are explained as intended, and the story does not end with lag that jumps on loop. It was captured with scripts/capture.mjs in iso and 2D (`--key v`), and scripts/drive.mjs seeked to the incident (window.__topo.story.seek) and shot it. Every PNG was looked at, and `node scripts/lines.mjs` reports `line ends: 0` in both views.

evals.prompt: can you make a diagram of our checkout request path for the design review? browser -> cloudfront -> ALB -> checkout-api (3 pods) -> redis (about 85% hit) and on a miss aurora postgres with one reader. checkout-api also calls the payments provider (stripe, slow, ~300ms). make it something people can poke at
evals.expected_output: The skill triggers even though the prompt never says isometric or simulation. A standalone HTML page from a spec with kinds that fit: client, cdn (with hit), lb, service with replicas: 3, cache, a db with role primary plus a replica fed by a replication edge, and an external node for Stripe with ms ≈ 300. Cache-aside is modelled with edge probabilities (api → redis p 1, api → aurora p ≈ 0.15); the latency readout (p50/p99) reflects Stripe's 300 ms on the critical path and the response says so. The figure is interactive: hover shows per-node stats, and clicking a node inspects it; F or the Fail/Restore button fails it. It has a short scenario that exercises the most useful failure for a design review, such as Redis down or Stripe slowing past a timeout, with narration, and the response explains what to try. --check was run and its numbers are quoted correctly. Iso and 2D were both captured and looked at, labels are readable and not hidden (no `label … is hidden` warning), and no edge passes under a node.

evals.prompt: Make a figure for our incident write-up showing how retries turned a slow inventory service into a full outage, and how adding a circuit breaker fixed it. The numbers: orders-api calls inventory with a 200 ms timeout and 3 retries; inventory normally answers in ~30 ms and can handle 300 req/s; during the incident a bad query made it take ~400 ms; normal load was ~200 req/s. Light theme, it's going on our internal wiki.
evals.expected_output: A standalone light page (`--light`) whose spec puts `timeout: 0.2`, `retries: 3` and a `backoff` on the orders-api → inventory edge, and gives inventory `ms: 30`, a capacity matching 300 req/s (in packets, scaled by sim.per) and a buffer (`queue`). The scenario has phases like steady → slowdown → breaker on → fixed. In the slowdown, a `set` step raises inventory's ms to ~400, so calls time out, amber retries multiply the load, the buffer fills and 503s appear. A later step adds a breaker with `set: { "orders>inventory": { breaker: … } }`, which trips open (red port) and turns the storm into fast failures. A final step restores ms, so the breaker half-opens and closes. --check shows the amplification and the recovery phase by phase; the response quotes those numbers rather than invented ones and explains that latency is model time. The story recovers before it loops, so there is no `ends failing` warning. A drive.mjs shot was taken at the storm and at the open breaker, and they were looked at in the light theme.

evals.prompt: We run active-active in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 behind Route 53 (TTL 60s). Each region: NLB, 4 api pods, a Postgres primary in us-east with a replica in eu-west over a ~80 ms link. I need a 2D diagram for the runbook that shows what a regional failover looks like. It should open in 2D, not the 3D look.
evals.expected_output: A spec with `view: "flat"`, so the page opens in 2D (the ISO switch still works). It has a dns node with route roundrobin and a ttl, two groups with `region: true` (each NLB → api with replicas → db), and cross-region replication carrying `ms: 80`. The TTL is either scaled down for watchability with the scaling stated in the caption, or kept honest and explained, but never silently changed. The scenario fails one region's load balancer, shows refused requests during the TTL window, the move of all traffic to the other region, and the restoration. Labels sit under each glyph without overlapping, region labels are readable, and lines.mjs reports 0 in the flat view. --check's per-phase failing rate and p99 are quoted in the caption.

evals.prompt: Show how we roll out a new checkout behind a feature flag: LaunchDarkly pushes config to the API gateway, the gateway sends the rollout % to checkout-v2 and the rest to checkout-v1, both write to the same orders DB. Show going 5% -> 25% -> 50%, v2 starting to throw errors at 50%, and us hitting the kill switch. Dark theme.
evals.expected_output: A spec with `flags: { <name>: { rollout: 0 } }`, a flags-kind node with a `kind: "config"` edge to the gateway, and a pair of edges from the gateway: one with `flag` to v2 and one with `unless` to v1. The scenario has named phases and flag steps (rollout 0.05 → 0.25 → 0.5), a `set` that gives v2 an `errorRate`, and a `kill` step. The flag panel's knob slides with the rollout, and the edge labels show the live split and the error percentage. --check shows the failing rate rising in the bad phase and dropping to ~0 after the kill. The response notes that the flag decision is per request and the same at every hop. Both themes or the requested dark theme were captured, with a shot at 50% showing red errors and the error-rate edge label.

A spec translated by hand from the compose file with sensible kinds: web as lb or gateway, api as service, worker as worker, db as db, cache as cache, and broker as queue (RabbitMQ is a queue with competing consumers, not a Kafka topic). Edges follow the real call direction (api publishes to the broker, and the worker consumes from it), not the depends_on direction. A client source is added with emit. Because the user gave no numbers, the response and the caption say plainly that the rates are illustrative, and the spec keeps them consistent (the worker keeps up at steady state). It includes a small scenario, for example the worker dying and the queue backing up then draining. --check passes, with any warning explained, and screenshots were read.

evals.prompt: just need a static svg of a simple 3-tier app for a slide: users, load balancer, 2 app servers, postgres primary + replica. isometric, dark. no animation needed
evals.expected_output: A static themed SVG from `node scripts/build.mjs <spec> --svg` (the <name>-iso.svg it writes), dark. It is a valid standalone SVG with width and height and its styles embedded, so it renders on its own in a slide or browser. The spec is small (client, lb, two services or one service with replicas: 2, db primary and replica with a replication edge), and the iso labels are readable and unhidden. The response gives the path to the SVG, notes that the HTML page with the live version also exists, and shows that the SVG was rendered (for example with scripts/capture.mjs) and looked at.

evals.prompt: Our payments topic is on 3 Kafka brokers, RF 3, min.insync.replicas 2, producers use acks=all. Partition 0 gets about half the traffic. My team doesn't get why losing ONE broker is fine but losing TWO stops all writes. Can you make something that shows it?
evals.expected_output: A spec whose kafka node has `brokers: 3, rf: 3, minIsr: 2, acks: "all"`, `skew` putting ~50% on partition 0, and a sync producer edge (so refused writes come back as errors) with a retry. The scenario has phases healthy → one broker down → two down → restored, failing brokers by id (`topic:b0`, then `topic:b1`). The narration explains the leader election pause (dimmed lane), why min ISR is still met with one broker down, and why acks=all refuses every write when only one in-sync replica is left. Broker units are clickable, so readers can try it themselves. --check shows writes refused (failing rate) only in the two-down phase. The hot partition's consumer load is sized so lag stays bounded at steady state. Screenshots in at least one view at the election and at the two-down moment were looked at.

evals.prompt: Show our orders API: POST writes Postgres and publishes an event; GET checks Redis and sometimes reads a replica. I want to inspect each route and follow one request.
evals.expected_output: Use an endpoint mix and endpoint calls with matching edges, records and tables. Describe cache reads as probabilistic unless genuinely sequenced. Click opens the inspector, route selection filters, Follow reveals spans. Disclose synthetic rates and keyspace; verify per-route numbers with --check and --trace. Capture both views and detail panels; line ends must be zero.

evals.prompt: Explain why saving my profile and immediately reading from a replica can show old data, and fix it by reading from the primary.
evals.expected_output: Use sequential upsert then select with then:true, a replica with scenario lag, and a fixed route reading the primary. Tune lag against the final layout. --check must show positive stale reads during the incident and zero once fixed; a followed incident request must show an older version or stale missing row. Do not invent exact versions. Inspect screenshots in both views and run line-end checks.

evals.prompt: Show why retrying a timed-out INSERT can conflict even though the first call failed, and what using a stable key and upsert changes.
evals.expected_output: Build an idempotent-retries story with actual edge timeouts and retries, synthetic records retained per request, insert then upsert routes, and a latency recovery. Verify a committed write followed by a retry conflict. State explicitly that upsert preserves row content, still writes versions/WAL, does not deduplicate external effects, and does not itself fix timeouts. Check conflict and failure rates by phase and inspect a trace and screenshots.

evals.prompt: Make an interactive explanation of lost updates when concurrent requests read and modify the same two rows, then show row locks fixing it.
evals.expected_output: Use rmw operations on two synthetic hot keys with long service time and a scenario enabling locks. --check must show lost updates before locking and zero after existing work drains, with lock waits visible. Disclose that version races are modeled, not SQL arithmetic or full transaction isolation. Inspect the database and both views, including zero line ends.

evals.prompt: Make a small profile API diagram where I can inspect all saved fields of one user: notification preferences, quota, enabled, and nickname. Show the write reaching a replica. Use synthetic values; I do not need a SQL editor.
evals.expected_output: Use documented records and tables with matching userId keys, endpoint upsert and a replication edge. Declare all requested fields in the spec, including false, zero and null values where relevant. Reuse the existing record inspector and Follow writes without modifying the engine or hardcoding fields in HTML. Verify saved fields at the primary and replica. Explain that the SELECT display is a read-only view of simulated storage and that field values are independently sampled. Run --check, inspect a browser screenshot and verify both view line ends.

evals.prompt: Show two tenant tiers sharing a gateway, routing to separate services and databases based on request metadata. Make a premium database outage stay isolated, and distinguish traffic with color.
evals.expected_output: Use workload, traffic, reusable policies and routing from the spec reference without engine edits. Route at two points from immutable context; include explicit fallback and real outgoing edges. Verify premium failure never falls back to standard storage. Use labeled named colors with Traffic/Activity/None controls and follow explanations. Run model checks, trace, browser screenshots in both views/themes and line ends.

evals.prompt: Show purchase and audit events sharing Kafka, a consumer outage and recovery, then each event reaching the appropriate downstream service.
evals.expected_output: Use mixed traffic workload and context; consumer routing chooses sinks after Kafka delivery. Context and class persist through backlog with parent/root trace continuity. Explain dispatch offsets rather than durable ACKs or exactly-once. Verify backlog drains, correct sinks receive each class, and follow includes async descendants. Inspect colors, reduced motion and phone layout; check browser console and line ends.

evals.prompt: Show one tenant-scoped order through a database write, Kafka event, search projection and Redis cache. Pause the consumer so I can inspect divergent saved fields and then follow recovery.
evals.expected_output: Uses entities and explicit endpoint entityStep bindings from the public spec reference. Scope isolates equal order IDs. Publication consumes an acknowledged committed snapshot, mappings rename saved fields, cache TTL is explicit. Captures a selected saved row with observed causal history and copy differences. Reports queued work, partial histories, and dispatch-only Kafka semantics. Runs check and browser verification in both views without custom engine changes.

evals.prompt: Add an optional search projection flag and roll it back while orders are queued. Existing admitted work should retain its decisions; new orders should skip search without failing the main save.
evals.expected_output: Uses optional entityStep on the projection call with modeled flag gates. Captures each decision on first encounter, retains it through asynchronous envelopes, and explains first encounter at a consumer versus producer. Shows skipped outcomes and copy divergence, tests trace disabled and flags disabled, and discloses that removing gates can run alternatives. Uses flagged-projection-rollout as an authoring example.
